definition: Internet slang meaning to arrange a casual sexual hookup with someone, typically via messaging apps or dating platforms; 炮 (pào, 'cannon') is crude slang for sex.
notes: 炮 as slang for sex is crude; 约炮 is ubiquitous on Chinese dating apps such as Momo. Predominantly mainland Chinese usage; Taiwanese speakers use different vocabulary.

definition: Literally 'one-night love/feeling'; the standard Mandarin term for a one-night stand with no expectation of ongoing contact.
notes: Emotional neutrality is slightly softened by 情 (feeling/love), giving it a faintly romantic framing absent from the English 'one-night stand'; otherwise a direct conceptual calque.

definition: Literally 'bedroom kung fu'; colloquial for sexual skill, stamina, and technique in bed, applicable to any gender.
notes: Maps imperfectly to sexual_potency (which centers on erectile function); the Chinese term emphasizes artistry and technique broadly. Plays on 功夫 (gōngfu, 'skill/martial arts') as a metaphor for sexual proficiency. Usually complimentary.

definition: Literally 'spring night'; a poetic and literary euphemism for a night of romantic or sexual intimacy, often evoking a wedding night or a passionate encounter.
notes: Derived from the Song-dynasty line 春宵一刻值千金 ('a spring night's moment is worth a thousand gold'). Connotations are romantic rather than crude; widely recognized through classical education and period drama.

definition: Literally 'to steal something fishy/rank-smelling'; colloquial for a married person sneaking out to have illicit sex; 腥 (fishy smell) is a crude oblique reference to sex.
notes: The fishy-smell allusion gives a mildly crude flavor to an otherwise casual idiom. Emphasizes stealth and illicitness over moral condemnation. Distinct from 出轨 in focusing specifically on the physical sexual act rather than the relational betrayal.

definition: Literally 'to go off the (train) rails'; the dominant modern Mandarin term for marital or relationship infidelity, covering both emotional and sexual cheating.
notes: Extremely common across all media and age groups. The railway metaphor implies straying from an established correct path. Applies to both emotional and sexual infidelity, unlike narrower terms.

definition: Literally 'a red apricot blossom grows over the garden wall'; a classical Chinese idiom specifically for a married woman committing adultery.
notes: From Song-dynasty poet Ye Shaoweng. Gender-specific: conventionally applied only to women; using it of a man is incongruous or ironic. Widely recognized through classical education and popular culture.

definition: Literally 'to steal a person'; colloquial for having a secret illicit sexual affair, with a stronger emphasis on physical (sexual) betrayal than 出轨.
notes: More vivid and slightly cruder than 出轨; common in vernacular speech and regional dialects. The 'stealing' framing implies both secrecy and active transgression. More likely to connote the sexual act itself.

definition: Literally 'nourishing to the eyes'; a compliment meaning someone or something is visually pleasing or attractive, often with implicit sexual or aesthetic appeal.
notes: Can be applied to people, scenery, or objects; when used of a person it implies attractiveness that may be sexual but need not be explicitly so. Very positive in connotation, essentially never offensive.

definition: Literally 'that thing'; a coy, evasive euphemism for the genitals — most commonly the penis — used to avoid naming the organ directly.
notes: The 儿 (er) retroflex suffix is a Northern Chinese (especially Beijing) dialectal marker, less common in southern dialects. Defaults to male genitalia but can refer to female genitalia in context. Used in a humorous or embarrassed register.

definition: 'Intimate relationship'; a semi-clinical euphemism used in media, public health, and everyday speech to refer to a romantic and/or sexual partnership without naming sex directly.
notes: Standard polite register for sex-inclusive partnerships; widely used by psychologists, journalists, and in formal writing. In legal or medical contexts can denote a single sexual act rather than an ongoing relationship.

definition: Literally 'to roll'; in sexual contexts an abbreviation of 滚床单 (gǔn chuángdān, 'to roll the sheets'), a crude colloquial euphemism for having sex.
notes: The primary meaning of standalone 滚 is an imperative ('get out / fuck off'). The sexual meaning is derived from the compound 滚床单 and requires explicit context to be read sexually. Recognition of the sexual-specific reading is substantially lower than overall recognition of the character as an expletive.

definition: Literally 'indescribable / cannot be described'; a Chinese internet euphemism for sexually explicit content or acts, deployed to evade content filters and censorship algorithms.
notes: Peaked circa 2013–2015 during early Weibo/WeChat censorship games. The irony is universal legibility: every reader knows exactly what is being alluded to. Functionally equivalent to NSFW but posed as mock modesty. Applies to any censored content, not only sexual.

definition: Literally 'you know (what I mean)'; a winking internet phrase used to imply sexual or otherwise sensitive content without stating it, relying on shared understanding between speaker and audience.
english_term: you know what I mean; wink wink
notes: Often followed by ellipsis or a knowing emoji. Applies to any sensitive topic but sexual implication is by far the most common usage. Low crude score because the referent is gestured at, not named.

definition: Literally 'those who know, all know'; a broader, slightly more exclusive version of 你懂的, implying that sexual or taboo content is self-evident to the initiated without spelling it out.
notes: More in-group than 你懂的; implies a community of knowing readers while excluding the uninitiated. Common in comment sections under ambiguously suggestive posts to signal sexual subtext while maintaining plausible deniability against content moderation.

definition: 'Ambiguous/flirtatious'; a state of romantic or sexual tension between two people who are undefined — neither a couple nor simply friends — characterized by pleasurable uncertainty and flirtatious signals.
notes: One of the most culturally loaded terms in modern Mandarin romance vocabulary; English lacks a single-word equivalent. Can describe the relationship status (处于暧昧, 'to be in an ambiguous state') or a specific flirtatious act (发暧昧, 'to send ambiguous signals'). Tone is usually positive or wistful rather than pejorative.

definition: Literally 'hidden rules'; an established Chinese term for the unwritten quid-pro-quo expectation that career advancement in entertainment, media, or business requires sexual compliance with power figures.
notes: Unlike the English 'casting couch' (individual predation), 潜规则 implies a normalized, systemic institutional arrangement in which the coercion is structural and widely understood. Reached peak salience during Chinese #MeToo discussions around 2018. Connotes both the predatory behavior and the complicit culture that sustains it.

definition: Literally 'inner meaning / connotation'; in Chinese internet usage, a genre tag for content containing hidden sexual meaning or double entendre perceptible only to the knowing reader.
notes: Primary meaning in standard Mandarin is 'depth of character / implicit meaning'; the sexual-subtext usage is a deliberate ironic repurposing by internet culture. Content tagged 内涵 typically appears innocent on the surface and relies on a shared code of references.

definition: Literally 'the closeness of skin touching skin'; a classical four-character euphemism for physical and sexual intimacy, implying naked bodily contact of a deeply intimate or sexual nature.
notes: The chengyu (four-character phrase) structure marks it as literary-classical register. Widely used in romance novels and period dramas to imply sex without explicit description. Does not necessarily imply full intercourse — can refer to any significant intimate skin contact.

definition: Literally 'the affection of fish in water'; a classical metaphor for the harmonious, mutually pleasurable sexual and emotional bond between a married couple — fish being perfectly at home in water.
notes: Classical in register; associated with traditional ideals of marital sexual harmony. Also appears extensively in Maoist political rhetoric (军民鱼水情, 'soldier-people fish-water affection'), which has diluted the specifically sexual connotation in modern usage.

definition: 'Secret/private liaison'; a clandestine sexual affair, typically adulterous or pre-marital, conducted in secret; carries connotations of moral and legal transgression.
notes: More formal or literary than 出轨; also carries a second meaning of 'secretly communicating with the enemy' (treason) in military/political contexts. The sexual meaning is older; both senses share the core notion of forbidden clandestine contact.

definition: Literally 'bedroom arts'; the classical Chinese (especially Taoist) tradition of sexual cultivation practices — including regulated intercourse, breath retention, and semen retention — believed to promote health, longevity, and spiritual development.
notes: A culturally distinct concept without a true English equivalent; Western 'tantric sex' is analogous but from an entirely different tradition. Referenced in texts such as 素女经 (Classic of the Plain Girl) and 玉房秘诀 (Secret Instructions of the Jade Chamber). Not a euphemism for sex — it is a genuine esoteric practice system with its own technical vocabulary.

definition: Classical Chinese: the act of an emperor sexually visiting and favoring a concubine or consort; the emperor 'gracing' a woman with his sexual attention, simultaneously conferring status upon her.
english_term: (imperial) to favor sexually; to be graced by the emperor
notes: Rooted in the Chinese imperial harem (后宫) system with no English equivalent. 'To bed a concubine' misses the unilateral power conferral — 幸 frames sex as a gift bestowed downward from absolute authority. The woman's consent or experience is structurally absent from the classical usage of the term.

definition: Literally 'to approach and favor'; classical Chinese for the emperor personally coming to a concubine's quarters for sex; 临 (to approach, condescend to be present) amplifies the power differential beyond standalone 幸.
english_term: (imperial) to personally favor sexually; to condescend with a sexual visit
notes: More specific than 幸 alone; 临 stresses the physical act of the emperor's arrival at a lesser person's location, further underscoring rank asymmetry. Found in imperial court records, historical annals, and period fiction. Shares the novel concept slug imperial_sexual_bestowal with 幸.

definition: Classical Chinese for lascivious over-familiarity or lecherous intimacy; taking unseemly sexual liberties with someone; blends contemptuous over-familiarity with sexual impropriety.
notes: Single-character classical term virtually absent from contemporary speech; encountered in classical texts and historical fiction. Appears in compounds such as 狎昵 (xíání, 'lascivious closeness') and 狎妓 (xiájì, 'to consort with prostitutes'). Low recognition reflects purely classical usage restricted to educated readers.
